title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook
author: Ava Martinez
summary: Consolidated reference covering the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes highlights, known issues, operational runbooks, and pointers to the team wiki.
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the authoritative design and operational guidance for Redwood Inference's Serving Runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, and platform owners. The playbook includes high-level architecture, kernel scheduling rationale, profiling and benchmarking procedures, release note highlights for runtime changes, known issues and mitigations, and day-2 runbooks with CLI snippets and dashboard links.

Scope and audience
- Scope: production serving runtime (GPU-accelerated inference engine), scheduling layer, profiling/benchmarking tooling, and operational runbooks.
- Audience: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, eng-infra, oncall rotation.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Purpose: provide a predictable, low-latency, high-throughput execution environment for language models with support for batching, KV-cache management, quantized kernels, and multi-tenant routing.

Key components:
- Request proxy (api-gateway): per-tenant auth, rate limits, input normalization, routing policies.
- Router & policy engine: selects model variant (fp16/int8/quantized), region, and queue (latency-priority vs throughput).
- Scheduler & batcher: continuous batching loop with workload-aware batch formation and admission control.
- Executor: GPU runtime with kernel selection, fused attention, rotary/ALiBi support, and KV cache.
- Cache service: prefix/KV caching with eviction policies and warmup hooks.
- Telemetry pipeline: streaming traces, token-level latency/timing, and per-kernel counters.

Service ownership
- api-gateway: api-team
- router & scheduler: serving-runtime
- executor/kernels: serving-runtime (kernel team)
- telemetry: eng-platform/observability

SLOs and targets (serving-runtime core)
- P99 tail latency (1k-token request): <= 2200 ms for latency-tier; <= 3500 ms for throughput-tier under 80th percentile load.
- P50 token-generation latency: <= 20 ms/token for medium models on A100-80GB equivalent.
- Instance availability: 99.95% monthly for Dedicated pools.
- Token error-rate (runtime exceptions): < 0.1%

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies

Goals: maximize GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs, avoid head-of-line blocking, and support graceful degradation between model variants.

Scheduling primitives:
- Work-stealing queues: per-GPU work queues with light-weight stealing to balance hot shards.
- Priority lanes: low-latency lane (small-batch, preemptible), throughput lane (large-batch, long-running).
- Admission control thresholds: max_pending_requests_per_gpu, max_batch_size, min_qos_reserved.

Default configuration (recommended)
| parameter | default (A100-equivalent) | notes |
|---|---:|---|
| max_batch_size | "256 tokens / 16 requests" | tuned by model size & seq len |
| max_pending_requests_per_gpu | "200" | safeguard for tail latency |
| low_latency_lane_qos | "reserved 20% GPU cycle" | ensures headroom for small requests |
| preemption_timeout_ms | "120" | allow small requests to preempt queued batches |

Preemption and fairness
- Small latency-sensitive requests can preempt queued throughput batches after preemption_timeout_ms.
- Leaky-bucket per-tenant guarantees to prevent burst starvation.

Kernel selection logic
1. Choose candidate kernel families by model architecture and quantization profile.
2. Score by: expected tokens/ms, memory headroom, KV cache friendliness.
3. Prefer fused kernels when sequence_length <= fused_threshold (default 1024).
4. Fall back to generic kernels when memory fragmentation or incompatible ops exist.

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile, collect signals, and triage)

When to profile:
- New model onboarding (first 3 production days).
- Release that changes kernel or scheduler (see release notes).
- Elevated tail latency or increased token error-rate.

Data to collect (minimum):
- Per-request trace: queue_time, batch_formation_time, kernel_exec_time, memcpy_h2d_ms, memcpy_d2h_ms, kv_cache_lookup_ms.
- Per-kernel counters: flops_estimate, kernel_time_ms, sm_efficiency, shared_memory_usage.
- GPU-level: GPU_util%, mem_used, cuda_pending_streams.
- Scheduling metrics: batch_sizes_histogram, preemptions_count, work_steals.

Profiling steps (lab-run):
1. Reproduce workload with the benchmark harness (see benchmarking suite).
2. Enable detailed tracing for a single GPU instance: set ENV PROFILE_LEVEL=2 and attach nsight or cupy-based sampling.
3. Run representative traffic for 10-30 minutes to capture steady-state and bursts.
4. Collect and upload traces to the trace viewer: s3://redwood-inference-profiles/{run-id}/.
5. Inspect waterfall: identify queue vs kernel time contributions.
6. If kernel_time dominates and SM efficiency < 30%, open issue for kernel team with run-id and perf dump.

Common triage checklist:
- High memcpy_h2d_ms: check input pre-processing path and zero-copy path flags.
- High queue_time: tune max_pending_requests_per_gpu or add capacity to latency-tier.
- Small batch sizes causing low throughput: increase batch_window_ms or adjust continuous-batching policy.
- Memory fragmentation: restart instance with full allocator reset and report to kernel team.

4) Benchmarking suite (harness and recommended workflows)

Purpose: reproduce production traffic patterns and measure tokens/sec, latency P50/P90/P99, and kernel-level metrics.

Components:
- workload-generator: python tool (bench/workload_generator.py) supporting trace replay and synthetic distributions.
- perf-collector: gathers traces, nvprof/nsys captures, and aggregates counters.
- comparison-report: generates CSV/Markdown reports and perf-diff artifacts.

Example commands:
- Generate synthetic mixed workload (70% short chat, 30% long completions):
  ./bench/workload_generator.py --profile mixed-chat --concurrency 120 --duration 600 --target endpoint://prod/model-v2

- Run perf-collector with nsight sampling:
  PROFILE_RUN=bench-mixed-2026-11-01 ./scripts/run_perf_collect.sh --out s3://redwood-inference-profiles/bench-mixed-2026-11-01

Baseline targets (A100-80GB equiv):
- Small-chat (<=128 tokens): P99 <= 180 ms (latency lane)
- Long-completion (>=1024 tokens): throughput >= 45 tokens/sec per GPU
- Embedding batch: throughput >= 400 requests/sec for 2048-d embeddings (batching enabled)

Reporting and CI integration
- Benchmarks for model onboarding must be posted to the onboarding PR and the model onboarding dashboard.
- Nightly bench runs: run against representative model set; failures (>=10% regression in tokens/sec or >50% P99 regression) create automatic alert and link to perf-diff.

5) Release notes (runtime changes callouts)

When runtime teams ship changes, include the following in the release notes:
- Summary of change (kernel/perf/scheduling), rationale, and owner.
- Impacted models/workloads and recommended mitigation (e.g., pin model to previous kernel).
- Benchmark diff artifacts and trace samples.
- Rollback instructions and feature flags.

Example release note snippet:
"2026-11-01: Introduced fused-attention-v2 kernel. Expected throughput +18% for medium models. Known limitations: high memory fragmentation for sequence lengths >4096; gate with FLAG_FUSED_V2. Owner: kernel-team@redwood."

6) Known issues and mitigations (operational)

Active issues:
- Issue KERN-172: intermittent CUDA launch failures on driver 525.x when fused-attention-v2 enabled. Mitigation: set FLAG_FUSED_V2=0 for affected pools; kernel-team investigating.
- Issue SCHED-89: starved latency-lane during sustained throughput bursts. Mitigation: increase low_latency_lane_qos to 30% and add preemption_timeout_ms=80.
- Issue CACHE-34: KV cache lookup latency spike due to Redis cluster GC. Mitigation: migrate hot shards to local in-memory cache for hot prefixes.

Escalation matrix:
1. Oncall identifies severity and follows runbook.
2. If GPU OOM or kernel crash impacting >1% of requests, page serving-runtime oncall.
3. If degraded availability >10 minutes or SLA risk, page eng-sre manager and CTO duty.

7) Runtime runbooks (day-2 operations)

Runbook: Elevated tail latency (P99 above SLO)
1. Check dashboards: p99_latency_per_model, queue_time_histogram, batch_size_histogram.
2. Run quick profiler for affected instance (portable):
   curl -XPOST http://INSTANCE/debug/profile?level=1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEBUG_TOKEN" -d '{}'
3. If queue_time > 50% of request time: scale out latency-tier nodes or adjust admission control.
4. If kernel_time high and SM efficiency low: tag instance, capture nsys trace, and escalate to kernel-team with run-id.
5. Mitigate by enabling fallback model variant (less quantized) or temporarily route to Dedicated pools.

Runbook: Kernel crash / CUDA error
1. Collect logs: /var/log/serving-runtime/executor.log and /var/log/nvidia/*.log.
2. Capture last 5 traces: curl http://INSTANCE/debug/traces?limit=5
3. Disable new kernel feature flag (FLAG_FUSED_V2=0) on affected autoscaling group and restart agent.
4. If OOM, reduce max_batch_size and coordinate with capacity planning.

8) Team wiki and knowledge resources

Canonical links (team wiki namespaces):
- Kernel playbook: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling-team-wiki
- Perf dashboards: dashboards/internal/serving-runtime-performance
- Onboarding checklist: confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/onboarding-checklist

How to contribute
- Propose changes via PR against this page: docs/serving-runtime/playbook/ and include benchmark artifacts.
- Tag reviewers: kernel-team, eng-sre, eng-platform.

Appendix A: Useful commands and snippets
- Restart executor on instance:
  sudo systemctl restart serving-executor
- Clear local allocator (safe downtime):
  curl -XPOST http://localhost:9000/admin/allocator/reset -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"
- Quick check for memory fragmentation (CUDA):
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -l 2

Appendix B: Example configuration fragment (YAML)
| key | value | description |
|---|---|---|
| scheduler.max_batch_size | "256" | maximum requests per batch (tokens-aware)
| scheduler.batch_window_ms | "12" | window to gather requests
| kernel.prefer_fused | "true" | prefer fused kernels when available
| scheduler.low_latency_qos_pct | "20" | reserved GPU cycles for latency lane

Appendix C: Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
1. Is this an application or runtime regression? Check model output diffs and token error-rate.
2. Has a new kernel or driver been rolled out recently? See release notes.
3. Are GPU metrics healthy? (util, mem, temperature)
4. If unknown, collect a perf trace and attach to ticket with labels: runtime/bug/perf.
